source_selection.grammar_source: three-tier: OMG normative XMI/JSON (A), Pilot Xtext (B), specification textual BNF transcription (B-prime)
source_selection.rationale: ADR-0010 chose a three-tier pin because no single source is both normative and machine-readable for the concrete syntax. Tier B-prime is an addition to that decision: SysML-v2-Release ships bnf/*.kebnf, a machine-readable transcription of the normative BNF that carries the specification's own clause numbers as comments. It supplies rule bodies and the spec-side production inventory for scripts/grammar_diff.py. It is NOT normative and does not displace the PDF: where the transcription and the clause disagree, the clause wins.

known_defects_going_in.defect: Encodes the pilot parser generator's LL limitations as though they were language rules: PackageBodyElement is manually inlined to avoid incremental parser loops, MultiplicityRange is narrowed because general bound expressions cause LL issues, and the -> and => syntactic predicates exist only to resolve ambiguity a recursive-descent parser does not have.
known_defects_going_in.consequence: Porting a rule body from the Xtext produces a parser that is less conformant while looking more conformant, because it agrees with the reference implementation. Invisible to a positive-only corpus sweep.
known_defects_going_in.mitigation: Rule bodies never come from Tier B. scripts/grammar_diff.py reports every inventory difference and the gate fails on an unreviewed one.

known_defects_going_in.defect: Self-declared as hand-corrected: the first line of each file reads "// Manual corrections by HP de Koning". It is a transcription of the PDF, not a normative artifact, and its corrections are not themselves traceable to a clause.
known_defects_going_in.consequence: A transcription error is indistinguishable from a specification rule when read out of the file alone. So is a silent correction of a real specification defect — which is not hypothetical: see the FlowFeatureRedefinition entry in deviations, where the transcription quietly repaired a dangling reference in the normative BNF and left no trace that the specification says otherwise.
known_defects_going_in.mitigation: The clause marker adjacent to each production is the citation, and the clause text is now retrievable — see source_selection.clause_retrieval. A production whose kebnf body cannot be reconciled with its clause is a conflict for the grammar-adjudicator agent, not a judgement call.

known_defects_going_in.defect: OMG issue KERML11-81 (https://issues.omg.org/issues/KERML11-81), open, filed 29 Aug 2025 by Ed Seidewitz (Model Driven Solutions): in the normative KerML.xmi each of the packages Connectors and Interactions has an association owning both of its ends, one named participantFeature, left over from TBD parts of earlier versions of the abstract syntax model. They should have been deleted and do not appear in the specification document. Verified against the live issue page, not recalled.
known_defects_going_in.consequence: The normative machine-readable artifact and the normative document disagree in at least one place, so neither can be treated as infallible.
known_defects_going_in.mitigation: Recorded here so a metaclass-map difference in those packages is expected rather than investigated as a defect. The issue is open, so the discrepancy in vendor/omg/20250201/KerML.xmi is expected to persist at this pin.

known_defects_going_in.defect: The ANTLR ports in circulation are known to carry defects that reject the specification's own examples.
known_defects_going_in.consequence: Not vendored. Recorded because it is the obvious alternative to Tier B and was considered and declined.

judgements.question: Is sysml/src/validation a negative corpus?
judgements.answer: No. Its files are named for modelling scenarios — 01-Parts Tree, 08-Requirements, 09-Verification — not for rule violations, so they are positive cases. Recorded because the directory name invites the opposite assumption, and treating 56 valid models as must-reject would make the sweep report nonsense.
judgements.confidence: read from the file names and directory structure, not from parsing them; a file here that fails to parse is to be investigated, not assumed invalid

judgements.question: ADR-0010 says 'Release repo examples'. Why are training/ and validation/ included?
judgements.answer: Tier C is defined in docs/DERIVATION.md as 'real files a conformant tool accepts', and all three trees are that. Excluding 156 real files to match a narrower word would weaken the corpus for no stated reason. This widens ADR-0010's wording; it does not change its decision.

judgements.question: Why is sysml.library/ excluded?
judgements.answer: The ten Tier A KPAR archives already contain the standard library as textual .sysml — verified by listing Systems-Library.kpar, which holds 'Systems Library/Parts.sysml' and siblings. Vendoring the Pilot's copy as well would put two standard libraries on disk with nothing stating which one the resolver may read.

tier_c_corpus.does_not_establish: Acceptance. corpus-sweep.sh needs a parser that accepts something and needs tests/rejection/, which is hand-written one case per rule violated with the clause cited (.claude/rules/tests.md). Neither exists yet, so the sweep is inert. A positive-only sweep is passed by a parser that accepts everything.

clause_retrieval.status: available; pinned by receipt, not by copy
clause_retrieval.what: Two closure-bounded LLM wikis built from the specification PDFs, consulted through the sysml-v2-wiki-navigator and kerml-wiki-navigator skills. They supply the clause TEXT that Tier B-prime only points at by number, which is what turns 'cite the clause' from an aspiration into a check.
clause_retrieval.validity: Both contain llms.txt, graph.sqlite and index/, which is the validity condition the skills state.
clause_retrieval.evidence_grade: Each atom carries a region_sha256 receipt binding it to a verbatim span of the source PDF, recorded with clause number, PDF page and printed page. That is strictly stronger than Tier B-prime, which has a clause number and no receipt.

coverage_measured.note: Every Tier B-prime production resolves to a wiki production atom at its own clause or an ancestor clause. Measured, not assumed.

cross_check_performed.method: For each clause present in both, compared the set of production names Tier B-prime assigns to it against the names defined in the wiki atom's verbatim BNF block.
cross_check_performed.caveat: The 25 are not 25 defects. Most are artefacts of the comparison: the wiki's PDF extraction flattens indentation, so assignment targets inside { ... } action blocks (originalPortDefinition, redefinedFeature, kind) parse as production heads. Each needs reading before it is called a difference. One real specification defect surfaced this way and is recorded in deviations.

limitations: The KerML wiki states that it is the pipeline output PLUS 11 hand-remediated atoms, and that it 'intentionally diverges from a fresh pipeline rebuild' — rebuilding reproduces the unremediated atoms. The remediation is documented as structural only, with content unchanged and the region_sha256 receipts still binding, and its content census passes 581/581. Recorded because a source that cannot be regenerated byte-identically is exactly what this repository refuses everywhere else.
The SysML wiki ships no REMEDIATIONS.md or audit report, so its remediation status is unstated rather than known-clean. The asymmetry with the KerML wiki is itself unexplained.

The skills are installed without the script they mandate: both SKILL.md files call ${CLAUDE_SKILL_DIR}/scripts/closure.py, and both skill directories contain only SKILL.md. The KerML script is in ~/.claude/scripts/closure.py (byte-identical to a copy in the user's Trash) and the SysML script is in ~/Downloads/sysml-v2-wiki-navigator-skill/. Retrieval works only when invoked by explicit path, so the contract the skills describe is not the contract an agent following them would execute.

A wiki is a third transcription, not the PDF. It is better-evidenced than Tier B-prime because of the receipts, and it is still not normative. L3 adjudication against build/regions.jsonl remains the last step for a genuine ambiguity.

Pinned by receipt only — see `pinning.what_this_does_not_buy`. The wikis themselves are not in the repository and a fresh clone cannot reproduce a citation without building them from the specification PDFs.

verified_by: .claude/scripts/build_wiki_receipts.py --check (the wikis on disk match the manifest)
scripts/check_citations.py (every receipt cited in this register is in the manifest)
pinning.what_is_recorded: Per atom: wiki, id, kind, clause, pdf_page, printed_page, region_sha256 (the wiki's receipt to the source PDF span) and file_sha256 (this repository's receipt to the rendered atom). Metadata only.
pinning.why_not_a_copy: The 1651 atoms carry roughly 2.3 MB of verbatim OMG specification prose and ship with no license or copyright notice. ADR-0010's 'IPR mode Non-Assert' is a patent position on the machine-readable artifacts, not a copyright license to redistribute specification text, and this repository is MIT and public. Receipts make a citation checkable without redistributing what it cites.
pinning.what_this_does_not_buy: A fresh clone still cannot build the wikis, so a clause citation is verifiable only on a machine that has them. That limit is inherent — the source PDFs are not redistributable either — and it is the honest residue of the earlier 'clause-retrieval-not-pinned' decision rather than a resolution of it. What changed is that drift is now detected and an invented receipt now fails a gate; what did not change is that the evidence base is not self-contained.

known_junk_in_pinned_inputs.what: The archives carry macOS packaging artefacts — .DS_Store entries and a __MACOSX/ tree, observed in Systems-Library.kpar.
known_junk_in_pinned_inputs.consequence: A library loader that walks archive entries indiscriminately will try to read them. Not a defect in the library; a defect waiting in any loader that assumes every entry is a model file.

deviations.upstream: The Xtext declares no rule of this name. KerMLExpressions.xtext implements the lexical level with a small set of terminals (ID, STRING_VALUE, DECIMAL_VALUE, EXP_VALUE, ML_NOTE, SL_NOTE, REGULAR_COMMENT, WS, UNRESTRICTED_NAME) whose regular expressions absorb this production rather than naming it.
deviations.problem: The specification states the lexical structure as named BNF productions, and `ALPHABETIC_CHARACTER` is one of them, defined at KerML 8.2.2.3. An Xtext terminal is a regular expression, so its sub-productions disappear into the regex and cannot appear in the Xtext inventory. The difference is one of formalism, not of what text is accepted.
deviations.rationale: Implement the lexical structure as the specification states it. A hand-written lexer is not bound by Xtext's terminal formalism, and naming these productions is what lets a rejection test cite the exact lexical rule an input violates, which one opaque terminal regex cannot do. Expect no separate parser function per production: the coverage marker belongs on the lexer routine implementing the clause.

deviations.upstream: The Pilot Xtext declares no rule named `ActionBehaviorMember`. Either it inlines this production into the rule that uses it, or it reaches the same construct under a different name.
deviations.problem: The specification states `ActionBehaviorMember` as a production of its own at SysML 8.2.2.17.1. A parser written from the Xtext inventory alone would not know this production exists, and its absence is invisible to a corpus sweep for as long as no pinned file exercises it.
deviations.rationale: Implement it. docs/DERIVATION.md states the resolution for this bucket: a specification-only production is usually one the Pilot has not implemented, and the specification is the normative source. Expect the corpus not to exercise it, which is exactly why it needs a rejection test rather than reliance on the sweep: a positive-only corpus cannot tell a production that is implemented from one that is missing.

deviations.upstream: Xtext defines `ActionDefKeyword: ActionKeyword 'def';`.
deviations.problem: A keyword factoring rule with no counterpart in the specification. Its body reduces to the literal sequence ['action', 'def'], which the specification does not name as a production — it writes those literals inline in ActionDefinition. The rule is an Xtext factoring convenience, not a language construct.
deviations.rationale: Do not create a production for this. The parser matches the literals directly where the specification writes them, so there is no rule here to mark for coverage and nothing is lost: the accepted input is identical either way. Porting the factoring would add a production the language does not have and would measure coverage against an inventory the specification does not recognise.

deviations.upstream: One level of the Xtext operator-precedence cascade, binding +, -. Its body delegates to the next tighter level and folds left-recursive repetitions in with a tree-rewrite action.
deviations.problem: The specification names no such production. It has one BinaryOperatorExpression for every infix operator and states precedence in a table at this clause, so `AdditiveExpression` is a rule shape standing in for a table entry — an artefact of the parser generator, not a construct of the language.
deviations.rationale: Implement the specification's shape: one BinaryOperatorExpression production whose operator comes from the BinaryOperator token set, with precedence supplied by the table at this clause and applied by the parser (precedence climbing, or an explicit table) rather than by the shape of the grammar. A recursive-descent parser written by hand does not need a rule per precedence level, and the cascade is not free: it is docs/DERIVATION.md's named example of an Xtext LL workaround, and porting it yields a parser that agrees with the reference implementation — and therefore looks more conformant — while describing a grammar the specification does not state. It would also report coverage against roughly twenty productions the language does not have, and make every precedence question a question about rule ordering rather than about the table, which is where the specification actually answers it.

evidence.ref: KerML 8.2.5.8.1 Operator Expressions (PDF p.120, printed p.94)
evidence.note: Retrieved as wiki production atom OperatorExpressions, region_sha256 423205c742ed7cc2… The clause states OwnedExpression as a flat alternation of ConditionalExpression, ConditionalBinaryOperatorExpression, BinaryOperatorExpression, UnaryOperatorExpression, ClassificationExpression, MetaclassificationExpression, ExtentExpression and PrimaryExpression — with no precedence cascade anywhere in it. Precedence for +, - belongs to the table at this clause, not to a production.

Xtext side read from the pinned grammar: the cascade is OwnedExpression -> ConditionalExpression -> NullCoalescingExpression -> ImpliesExpression -> OrExpression -> XorExpression -> AndExpression -> EqualityExpression -> ClassificationExpression -> RelationalExpression -> RangeExpression -> AdditiveExpression -> MultiplicativeExpression -> ExponentiationExpression -> UnaryExpression -> ExtentExpression, each level eliminating left recursion with an Xtext tree-rewrite action of the form {SysML::OperatorExpression.operand += current}. That action is a parser-generator construct with no counterpart in the specification's notation.

Xtext side read from the pinned grammar: the cascade is OwnedExpression -> ConditionalExpression -> NullCoalescingExpression -> ImpliesExpression -> OrExpression -> XorExpression -> AndExpression -> EqualityExpression -> ClassificationExpression -> RelationalExpression -> RangeExpression -> AdditiveExpression -> MultiplicativeExpression -> ExponentiationExpression -> UnaryExpression -> ExtentExpression, each level eliminating left recursion with an Xtext tree-rewrite action of the form {SysML::OperatorExpression.operand += current}. That action is a parser-generator construct with no counterpart in the specification's notation.

deviations.rationale: KERML11-181 quotes this exact clause and states the FeatureDeclaration reference should be optional. deviations.upstream: vendor/pilot/SysML.xtext (lines 2436-2439) overrides `ExpressionBody returns SysML::Expression : CalculationBody`, so every SysML expression body, including select, collect and forAll bodies, reads SysML's calculation body.
deviations.problem: SysML does not state ExpressionBody. Taken literally, it falls back to KerML 8.2.5.8.3, `ExpressionBody : Expression = '{' FunctionBodyPart '}'`, whose TypeBodyElement and ReturnFeatureMember (KerML 8.2.5.7.1) reach the KerML kernel. A SysML `{ ... }` expression body would then contain KerML elements, and SysML usages would be rejected in it.
deviations.rationale: Decided by the corpus, with the pilot agreeing. `vendor/corpus/sysml/src/validation/07-Variant Configuration/7b-Variant Configurations.sysml` line 127, `rearWheelChoice->forAll {in ref w; w == rearWheelChoice::narrowRimWheel}`, and `15-Properties-Values-Expressions/15_05-Unification of Expression and Constraint Definition.sysml` line 9, `wheelAssy->forAll {in ref w: WheelAssy;`, put `ref` in an expression body parameter. `ref` is SysML's usage prefix; KerML's BasicFeaturePrefix (8.2.4.3.1) has no such option. So these cannot parse under KerML's body. SysML itself states CalculationBody (8.2.2.19) as `';' | '{' CalculationBodyPart '}'` over SysML's ActionBodyItem, and the pilot routes every expression body through it. SysML's statement that it uses 'the expression notation from [KerML]' covers the operator and primary layer, and nothing in SysML says expression bodies hold KerML kernel elements. No OMG issue settles it; SysML and KerML trackers were searched on 2026-09-17. Adjudicated by the grammar-adjudicator on 2026-09-17; the corpus lines and KerML's BasicFeaturePrefix were checked directly. NARROWED on 2026-09-23 (pending decision expression-body-semicolon, settled): the reading is CalculationBody's braced alternative alone, `'{' CalculationBodyPart '}'`. The bare `;` alternative is not read as an expression body, because taken literally it makes `attribute x = ;;` an attribute valued by an empty body and `a->f;` a complete operation, and the corpus that is this deviation's evidence writes every expression body braced.

deviations.upstream: SysML.xtext (and KerML.xtext) define `FilterPackageImport: FilterPackageMembershipImport | FilterPackageNamespaceImport`, whose two helpers are ImportedMembership and ImportedNamespace. They admit the same import forms without the nested-FilterPackage alternative of NamespaceImport.
deviations.problem: SysML 2.0 clause 8.2.2.5.1 uses FilterPackageImport in `FilterPackage : Package = ownedRelationship += FilterPackageImport ( ownedRelationship += FilterPackageMember )+` and never defines it. The PDF (page 199, printed 167) goes from FilterPackage straight to FilterPackageMember. As printed, SysML's filter-package syntax cannot be derived from the normative clause.
deviations.rationale: Take the definition from the specification's own machine-readable BNF, Tier B' (vendor/spec-bnf/SysML-textual-bnf.kebnf line 172, clause 8.2.2.5.1): `FilterPackageImport : Import = ImportDeclaration { visibility = 'public' }`. It is not normative, but it is the specification's transcription, not the pilot's. KerML 8.2.3.4.2's FilterPackage uses ImportDeclaration directly, so the two languages then accept the same filter-package syntax. OMG has the omission as SYSML21-449, 'Undefined rules in the text notation grammar', which names FilterPackageImport as referenced on page 200 and undefined. The pilot's two helpers accept the same token sequences: a nested filter package only adds further bracketed members. So following Tier B' changes structure, not the language. Revisit when SYSML21-449 is resolved. The same issue names CalculationUsageDeclaration as undefined (page 188), which will need the same treatment when its unit comes up.

KERML11-181 was fetched and read in full: it names only 8.2.5.7.2 Expression and 8.2.5.7.4 BooleanExpression/Invariant, not Flow or 8.2.5.9.2. deviations.upstream: vendor/pilot/SysML.xtext (lines 1325-1330) writes FlowEndSubsetting's first alternative as `referencedFeature = [SysML::Feature | QualifiedName] '.'`, with the trailing '.' the specification omits.
deviations.problem: SysML 8.2.2.16 states FlowEndSubsetting = referencedFeature = [QualifiedName] | referencedFeature = FeatureChainPrefix, and FlowEnd = FlowEndSubsetting? FlowFeatureMember. QualifiedName separates segments with '::' only (KerML 8.2.3.4.1), and FeatureChainPrefix, ( OwnedFeatureChaining '.' )+ OwnedFeatureChaining '.', needs at least two chainings and two dots. So a two-segment end such as `p1.torque` has nowhere for its dot: the first alternative would read `from p1 torque`, and the second needs `a.b.` before the flow feature.
deviations.rationale: The dot is missing from the first alternative, not optional: nothing else in the clause can consume it, and SysML's own KerML base states FlowEnd with the dot (KerML 8.2.5.9.2, ( OwnedReferenceSubsetting '.' )? FlowFeatureMember). The corpus uses the two-segment form throughout; the adjudicator counted 121 flow ends of that shape, among them the Annex A model's first flow, `flow p1.torque to p2.torque;`. Three-segment ends parse through FeatureChainPrefix as written, so only the first alternative changes. No open SysML issue title names FlowEnd, FlowEndSubsetting or FeatureChainPrefix (the open list was read on 2026-09-17); closed issues were not searched. Adjudicated by the grammar-adjudicator on 2026-09-17; the clause, Xtext and corpus line were rechecked directly.

deviations.upstream: The Pilot Xtext has no FlowFeatureRedefinition rule at all. SysML.xtext:1320 and :1333 build a FlowFeatureMember and reach the redefinition by another route, so the production is absent rather than spelled differently.
deviations.problem: The normative BNF contradicts itself here. Within clause 8.2.2.16 the specification REFERENCES the production as FlowFeatureRedefinition ('ownedRelationship += FlowFeatureRedefinition') and one line later DEFINES it as 'FlowFeatureRefefinition : Redefinition =' — Refefinition, with an f where the d belongs. Read literally, the clause contains a dangling reference: nothing defines FlowFeatureRedefinition, and nothing references FlowFeatureRefefinition. The Tier B-prime transcription silently repairs the definition to FlowFeatureRedefinition and leaves no mark that the specification says otherwise, which is how a reader comes to believe the spelling is settled.
deviations.rationale: Follow the specification's own reference, FlowFeatureRedefinition, and treat the definition line as the defect. The reference is the load-bearing occurrence: FlowFeature's body cites it, so taking the definition's spelling as authoritative would leave FlowFeature pointing at nothing. The corrected spelling also matches the surrounding Redefinition vocabulary and the metaclass the rule constructs. Adopting the typo would reproduce a defect that the grammar cannot actually mean. The Xtext casts no vote, having neither spelling, but KerML does: it spells the production correctly in both positions. Already on file upstream and still open; the issue is cited in the evidence.

Not an extraction artefact: the same atom renders 'Redefinition' correctly two lines earlier, so the extractor is plainly capable of the word.

KerML 8.2.5.9.2 Flows (wiki production atom Flows, region_sha256 150b0ccc1e0d5422…) spells the production `FlowFeatureRedefinition` in BOTH places — the reference inside FlowFeature and the definition line — so the base language, which SysML's flow notation is layered on, has no typo. That removes the remaining doubt about which spelling was intended: only the SysML document's definition line reads Refefinition, and it is alone against its own reference one line above and against KerML's two.

Tier B-prime reads 'FlowFeatureRedefinition : Redefinition =' — the corrected spelling, applied without comment. This is a concrete instance of the 'Manual corrections by HP de Koning' header operating invisibly.
The SysML v2 Tier A pin the clause belongs to. Recorded so the claim moves if the pin moves.

PARTIAL MATCH. 'Typos: Namspace, Refefinition, Relationsuip, Relationsup, Eleemnt' (https://issues.omg.org/issues/SYSML21-399), open, filed 27 Oct 2025 by Kent Johnson (Emerson) against SysML 2.0. It lists 'Refefinition: 179' — one page off from our 178, consistent with the same occurrence given FlowFeatureRedefinition sits ~82 lines after FlowDefinition in the same clause. The issue reports it purely as a SPELLING typo: it does not name the production and does not record the consequence, that the clause is left with a dangling reference because nothing defines the name FlowFeature cites. That framing is unreported upstream.

The sibling defect in this clause, `FlowDefinition :` with no '=', is EXACT MATCH item 7 of SYSML21-402 (https://issues.omg.org/issues/SYSML21-402), open, at page 178 — our page exactly. Note that SYSML21-402 does NOT list the Refefinition misspelling and SYSML21-399 does not list FlowDefinition, so the two defects in clause 8.2.2.16 are on file as two separate issues.

deviations.upstream: One level of the Xtext operator-precedence cascade, binding implies. Its body delegates to the next tighter level and folds left-recursive repetitions in with a tree-rewrite action.
deviations.problem: The specification names no such production. It has one BinaryOperatorExpression for every infix operator and states precedence in a table at this clause, so `ImpliesExpression` is a rule shape standing in for a table entry — an artefact of the parser generator, not a construct of the language.
deviations.rationale: Implement the specification's shape: one BinaryOperatorExpression production whose operator comes from the BinaryOperator token set, with precedence supplied by the table at this clause and applied by the parser (precedence climbing, or an explicit table) rather than by the shape of the grammar. A recursive-descent parser written by hand does not need a rule per precedence level, and the cascade is not free: it is docs/DERIVATION.md's named example of an Xtext LL workaround, and porting it yields a parser that agrees with the reference implementation — and therefore looks more conformant — while describing a grammar the specification does not state. It would also report coverage against roughly twenty productions the language does not have, and make every precedence question a question about rule ordering rather than about the table, which is where the specification actually answers it.

KerMLExpressions.xtext implements the lexical level with a small set of terminals (ID, STRING_VALUE, DECIMAL_VALUE, EXP_VALUE, ML_NOTE, SL_NOTE, REGULAR_COMMENT, WS, UNRESTRICTED_NAME) whose regular expressions absorb this production rather than naming it.
deviations.problem: The specification states the lexical structure as named BNF productions, and `LINE_TERMINATOR` is one of them, defined at KerML 8.2.2.1. An Xtext terminal is a regular expression, so its sub-productions disappear into the regex and cannot appear in the Xtext inventory. The difference is one of formalism, not of what text is accepted.

A hand-written lexer is not bound by Xtext's terminal formalism, and naming these productions is what lets a rejection test cite the exact lexical rule an input violates, which one opaque terminal regex cannot do. Expect no separate parser function per production: the coverage marker belongs on the lexer routine implementing the clause.

deviations.problem: KerML 8.2.5.13 and SysML 8.2.2.5.1 both print `( isStandard ?= 'standard' ) 'library' ...` with no '?' on the group, which makes 'standard' mandatory and isStandard always true. deviations.rationale: The printed rule contradicts the specification around it. KerML 7.4.14 gives `library package AddressBooks {` without 'standard' and says only library packages from the Kernel Model Libraries or other recognized standard libraries should be identified as standard. The LibraryPackage metaclass (8.3.4.13.3) says isStandard 'should only be set to true' for those libraries, so false must be writable. The adjudicator found that the BNF's other standalone flag groups (isAbstract, isDerived, isReference, isImportAll and the rest) carry the trailing '?', and a bare `x ?= 'kw'` appears only where the keyword is the fixed opener of an alternative, which 'standard' is not. The corpus writes `library package` without 'standard' 9 times and never with it; the adjudicator reports that the pinned Tier A standard-library KPARs open with `standard library package` throughout. SysML restates KerML's text word for word, so it is one defect printed twice. The adjudicator read the KerML and SysML issue pages on 2026-09-17 and found no issue naming it; KERML11-10 (the keyword table) and SYSML21-267 (graphical notation) were read and are not about this. The pages may list open issues only, so the search is not conclusive, and no issue is cited. Adjudicated by the grammar-adjudicator on 2026-09-17; the 7.4.14 and 8.3.4.13.3 wording and the corpus lines were rechecked directly.

deviations.rationale: Implement the specification's shape: one BinaryOperatorExpression production whose operator comes from the BinaryOperator token set, with precedence supplied by the table at this clause and applied by the parser (precedence climbing, or an explicit table) rather than by the shape of the grammar. A recursive-descent parser written by hand does not need a rule per precedence level, and the cascade is not free: it is docs/DERIVATION.md's named example of an Xtext LL workaround, and porting it yields a parser that agrees with the reference implementation — and therefore looks more conformant — while describing a grammar the specification does not state. The KerML-only `Identification ValuePart` alternative is outside the defect and is kept. The corpus has typing-first payloads (`flow of Fuel from ...`, `flow call_getItems of CallGiveItems[1]`) and no payload that is a multiplicity alone or multiplicity-first, so it does not decide the disputed alternative either way; a negative case for `flow of [2] from a to b;` is therefore warranted. deviations.rationale: Implement the specification's shape: one BinaryOperatorExpression production whose operator comes from the BinaryOperator token set, with precedence supplied by the table at this clause and applied by the parser (precedence climbing, or an explicit table) rather than by the shape of the grammar. KerMLExpressions.xtext implements the lexical level with a small set of terminals (ID, STRING_VALUE, DECIMAL_VALUE, EXP_VALUE, ML_NOTE, SL_NOTE, REGULAR_COMMENT, WS, UNRESTRICTED_NAME) whose regular expressions absorb this production rather than naming it.
deviations.problem: The specification states the lexical structure as named BNF productions, and `SINGLE_LINE_NOTE` is one of them, defined at KerML 8.2.2.2. deviations.rationale: Implement the lexical structure as the specification states it. Expect no separate parser function per production: the coverage marker belongs on the lexer routine implementing the clause.

deviations.upstream: vendor/pilot/KerML.xtext (lines 323-328) writes TypeDeclaration's ( SpecializationPart | ConjugationPart ) group exactly once, with no quantifier.
deviations.problem: KerML 8.2.4.1.1 prints the group as ( SpecializationPart | ConjugationPart )+, which admits `type A :> B ~ C;` and `type A ~ B ~ C;`. The Xtext admits one part only. Both require at least one part, so `type A;` is rejected by both and is not in dispute. The models the '+' additionally admits are invalid: validateTypeAtMostOneConjugator (KerML 8.3.3.1.10) allows at most one owned Conjugation, and KerML 7.3.2.4 says a conjugated type cannot be the specific type of a Specialization. KerML 7.3.2.2 describes a type declaration as defining 'either one or more owned specializations ... or a conjugator'.
deviations.rationale: Keep the printed '+' and leave the two rules to validation. The Xtext's single occurrence has no LL motive, as the adjudicator found; it encodes validation constraints in syntax, which is the same move this repository declined in PrefixMetadataTyping-chain: a requirement the specification states as a constraint parses and fails at validation, because validity gates writes, not reads (ADR-0002). Here the constraints are structural rather than name-resolving, which makes the syntactic narrowing possible but not required. KerML 7.3.2.2's 'either ... or' describes a valid model, and validateTypeAtMostOneConjugator says the same thing as a constraint; neither is a grammar rule. The printed clause and the Tier B' transcription (kebnf line 399) agree on '+'. The corpus is silent on the disputed forms: every type declaration in it has exactly one part, e.g. Simple Tests/Types.kerml lines 2-29, so a parser following either reading accepts it all. deviations.problem: The specification names no such production. It has one BinaryOperatorExpression for every infix operator and states precedence in a table at this clause, so `UnaryExpression` is a rule shape standing in for a table entry — an artefact of the parser generator, not a construct of the language.
deviations.rationale: Implement the specification's shape: one BinaryOperatorExpression production whose operator comes from the BinaryOperator token set, with precedence supplied by the table at this clause and applied by the parser (precedence climbing, or an explicit table) rather than by the shape of the grammar. A recursive-descent parser written by hand does not need a rule per precedence level, and the cascade is not free: it is docs/DERIVATION.md's named example of an Xtext LL workaround, and porting it yields a parser that agrees with the reference implementation — and therefore looks more conformant — while describing a grammar the specification does not state. It would also report coverage against roughly twenty productions the language does not have, and make every precedence question a question about rule ordering rather than about the table, which is where the specification actually answers it.

deviations.upstream: The Xtext declares no rule of this name. KerMLExpressions.xtext implements the lexical level with a small set of terminals (ID, STRING_VALUE, DECIMAL_VALUE, EXP_VALUE, ML_NOTE, SL_NOTE, REGULAR_COMMENT, WS, UNRESTRICTED_NAME) whose regular expressions absorb this production rather than naming it.
deviations.problem: The specification states the lexical structure as named BNF productions, and `WHITE_SPACE` is one of them, defined at KerML 8.2.2.1. An Xtext terminal is a regular expression, so its sub-productions disappear into the regex and cannot appear in the Xtext inventory. The difference is one of formalism, not of what text is accepted.
deviations.rationale: Implement the lexical structure as the specification states it. A hand-written lexer is not bound by Xtext's terminal formalism, and naming these productions is what lets a rejection test cite the exact lexical rule an input violates, which one opaque terminal regex cannot do. Expect no separate parser function per production: the coverage marker belongs on the lexer routine implementing the clause.

deviations.problem: No production of this name in the specification, which states `WHITE_SPACE = space | tab | form_feed | LINE_TERMINATOR` at KerML 8.2.2.1 Line Terminators and White Space. NOT merely a naming difference. The specification lists FOUR kinds of white space and the Xtext accepts three: form_feed (U+000C) is absent from the Pilot terminal. A source file separating tokens with a form feed is well-formed by the specification and is a lexical error for the Pilot. This is a real conformance gap in the reference implementation, not a formalism difference, and it is exactly the kind of divergence a positive-only corpus sweep can never surface — no pinned corpus file is likely to contain a form feed.
deviations.rationale: Follow the specification: accept form feed as white space. The Pilot is not normative and its terminal is narrower than the clause, so matching the Pilot here would import a conformance gap while appearing to agree with the reference implementation — the precise failure docs/DERIVATION.md warns about. Needs a positive test containing a form-feed-separated token, because no corpus file is likely to exercise it and the sweep will therefore stay silent either way.

deviations.upstream: One level of the Xtext operator-precedence cascade, binding xor. Its body delegates to the next tighter level and folds left-recursive repetitions in with a tree-rewrite action.
deviations.problem: The specification names no such production. It has one BinaryOperatorExpression for every infix operator and states precedence in a table at this clause, so `XorExpression` is a rule shape standing in for a table entry — an artefact of the parser generator, not a construct of the language.
deviations.rationale: Implement the specification's shape: one BinaryOperatorExpression production whose operator comes from the BinaryOperator token set, with precedence supplied by the table at this clause and applied by the parser (precedence climbing, or an explicit table) rather than by the shape of the grammar. A recursive-descent parser written by hand does not need a rule per precedence level, and the cascade is not free: it is docs/DERIVATION.md's named example of an Xtext LL workaround, and porting it yields a parser that agrees with the reference implementation — and therefore looks more conformant — while describing a grammar the specification does not state. It would also report coverage against roughly twenty productions the language does not have, and make every precedence question a question about rule ordering rather than about the table, which is where the specification actually answers it.

deviations.upstream: SysML.xtext:1632 writes `ownedRelatedElement += ForVariableDeclaration`, routing through the ReferenceUsage-producing wrapper the clause itself defines, rather than assigning UsageDeclaration directly.
deviations.problem: SysML 8.2.2.17.7 states `ForVariableDeclarationMember : FeatureMembership = ownedRelatedElement += UsageDeclaration`. UsageDeclaration is not an element: the pilot declares it `fragment UsageDeclaration returns SysML::Usage` (SysML.xtext:596), a fragment contributing features to whatever object its caller is building rather than instantiating one of its own, so it cannot be the target of a list-valued element assignment. Read literally the clause also leaves its own ForVariableDeclaration, defined two lines below as `ReferenceUsage = UsageDeclaration`, referenced by nothing — the only unreachable production in the SysML grammar.
deviations.rationale: A transcription slip in the clause, not a pilot workaround, and the specification's own text is what shows it. Its three siblings in the same clause each assign an element-producing production — ExpressionParameterMember to OwnedExpression, ActionBodyParameterMember to ActionBodyParameter, IfNodeParameterMember to IfNode — and ForVariableDeclarationMember is the only one that does not. Clause 8.2.2.6.2 states the identical shape this production should have: `OwnedCrossFeatureMember : OwningMembership = ownedRelatedElement += OwnedCrossFeature` over `OwnedCrossFeature : ReferenceUsage = BasicUsagePrefix UsageDeclaration`, a membership assigning a ReferenceUsage wrapper of UsageDeclaration, which is exactly what ForVariableDeclaration already is. And the string `ownedRelatedElement += UsageDeclaration` occurs in exactly one clause of the whole pinned export, this one — verified over all 558 clauses, not sampled. Both readings accept identical text, so nothing about the language turns on it; what turns on it is whether the specification's own ForVariableDeclaration is reachable or permanently orphaned. No OMG issue names either production: the SysML issue list was fetched and searched on 2026-09-17 and has no match, so none is cited. Adjudicated by the grammar-adjudicator on 2026-09-17; the fragment declaration and the single-occurrence count were re-verified before this entry was written.

evidence.note: States `ForVariableDeclarationMember : FeatureMembership = ownedRelatedElement += UsageDeclaration` and, two lines below, `ForVariableDeclaration : ReferenceUsage = UsageDeclaration`.

The precedent the specification sets for this shape: `OwnedCrossFeatureMember : OwningMembership = ownedRelatedElement += OwnedCrossFeature` over `OwnedCrossFeature : ReferenceUsage = BasicUsagePrefix UsageDeclaration`. A membership assigns the wrapper, never UsageDeclaration itself.

Line 32 `for n : ScalarValues::Integer in (1, 2, 3) {` is the sole corpus instance and does NOT separate the two readings: both consume the same text. Recorded so that no later reader mistakes corpus silence here for corpus support.
